# What are hallucinations? 🤔 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Defining AI hallucination

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Hallucination]{.alert}: When an AI generates **plausible‑sounding but incorrect or nonsensical** content
- Not just mistakes—[confidently wrong]{.alert} outputs
- Coined by researchers to describe LLM “fabrications”
- Analogous to human [confabulation]{.alert}: filling gaps with invented details
- Examples:
  - Inventing non‑existent books, papers, or events
  - Providing false citations
  - Making up biographical details
  - Contradicting established facts
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Hallucination example: banana phone](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [OpenAI](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8313428-does-chatgpt-tell-the-truth)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The creativity–hallucination spectrum

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Same underlying mechanism can produce both [harmful errors]{.alert} and [valuable creativity]{.alert}
- **Creativity**: novel, useful, and appropriate ideas
- **Hallucination**: novel, but **inaccurate or inappropriate**
- The line is often [context‑dependent]{.alert}
  - Fiction writing → creativity
  - Medical advice → dangerous hallucination
- Key question: [Can we harness the creativity while minimising the harm?]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Spectrum from creativity to hallucination](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [Jiang et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06647)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Why do LLMs hallucinate?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Training data noise**: Models learn from imperfect, contradictory, or outdated sources
- **Statistical generation**: LLMs predict the next token based on probability, not truth
- **Lack of grounding**: No direct connection to reality or external knowledge
- **Over‑generalisation**: Applying patterns where they don’t belong
- **Instruction following**: Trying to please the user even when uncertain
- **Short‑term memory**: Limited context window leads to inconsistency
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![LLM generating false information](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallucination_(artificial_intelligence))
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Types of hallucinations 📊 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Factual hallucinations

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Factual errors**: Statements that contradict verifiable facts
  - “The Eiffel Tower is in London.”
  - “Shakespeare wrote *1984*.”
- **Citation fabrication**: Inventing papers, authors, or URLs
  - “According to Smith et al. (2023)…”
  - (No such paper exists)
- **Temporal errors**: Wrong dates, anachronisms
  - “The iPhone was released in 1995.”
- **Numerical errors**: Incorrect statistics, numbers
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Factual hallucination example](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [OpenAI](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8313428-does-chatgpt-tell-the-truth)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Logical and coherence hallucinations

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Logical inconsistencies**: Self‑contradiction within the same response
  - “The meeting is at 3 pm. It will start at 4 pm.”
- **Nonsensical output**: Grammatically correct but meaningless
  - “The quadratic chicken paradoxically sings under the moon.”
- **Contextual drift**: Losing track of the topic or user’s intent
- **Over‑specification**: Adding unnecessary, made‑up details
  - “The 2019 study by Dr. Jane Doe (University of Oxford, pp. 45‑67) showed…”
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Logical inconsistency example](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [Programmer Humor](https://programmerhumor.io/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Intentional vs. unintentional hallucinations

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
**Unintentional (most common)**
- Model genuinely “believes” its output is correct
- Arises from training data or architectural limitations
- Can be reduced with better training, retrieval, etc.

**Intentional (rare)**
- Model deliberately generates false information
- May occur in adversarial settings (jailbreaks)
- Could be used for disinformation or manipulation
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
**The grey area**
- **Useful fiction**: Storytelling, brainstorming, hypotheticals
- **Plausible deniability**: “I’m not sure, but perhaps…”
- **Creative elaboration**: Adding colour to a narrative
- **Educational simplification**: Oversimplifying complex topics
:::
:::

:::{.fragment}
:::{style="margin-top: 20px; text-align: center;"}
> The same mechanism that produces a brilliant poem can also produce a dangerous medical misdiagnosis.
:::
:::
:::

# Measuring hallucinations 📏 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## How do we know if an LLM is hallucinating?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Human evaluation**: Experts compare output to ground truth
  - Gold standard, but expensive and slow
- **Automatic metrics**:
  - **Fact‑checking**: Use knowledge bases (Wikipedia, Wikidata)
  - **Consistency checks**: Compare multiple generations
  - **Entailment models**: Determine if output contradicts source
  - **Perplexity**: Unexpected token sequences may indicate nonsense
- **Benchmarks**:
  - [TruthfulQA](https://github.com/sylinrl/TruthfulQA): Tests tendency to mimic human falsehoods
  - [HaluEval](https://github.com/RUCAIBox/HaluEval): Hallucination evaluation dataset
  - [FActScore](https://github.com/shmsw25/FActScore): Factual accuracy scoring
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Hallucination evaluation pipeline](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [Jiang et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06647)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The challenge of evaluation

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Ground truth may be ambiguous**: Some questions have multiple correct answers
- **Temporal dynamics**: Facts change over time (what was true yesterday may be false today)
- **Context dependence**: A statement may be true in one context but false in another
- **Partial hallucinations**: Only part of the output is wrong
- **Subtle errors**: Hard for non‑experts to detect
- **Scalability**: Need automated methods for large‑scale evaluation
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Evaluation challenges](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06647)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Mitigation strategies 🛡️ {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG)

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [RAG]{.alert}: Ground LLM responses in external, verifiable sources
- **How it works**:
  1. Retrieve relevant documents from a knowledge base
  2. Inject those documents into the prompt as context
  3. Generate answer based on retrieved context
- **Benefits**:
  - Reduces factual hallucinations by providing evidence
  - Allows updating knowledge without retraining
  - Provides citations for verification
- **Limitations**:
  - Retrieval may fail to find relevant information
  - LLM may still ignore or misinterpret retrieved content
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![RAG pipeline](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [Lewis et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Fine‑tuning and alignment

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Supervised fine‑tuning (SFT)**: Train on high‑quality, fact‑checked examples
- **Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)**: Reward model for truthful, helpful, harmless outputs
- **Constitutional AI**: Train models to follow principles that discourage hallucination
- **Process‑based supervision**: Reward each step of reasoning, not just final answer
- **Self‑consistency techniques**: Generate multiple answers and pick the most consistent
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![RLHF reduces hallucination](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/learning-from-human-preferences/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Prompt engineering techniques

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
**Explicit instructions**
- “Be accurate and cite sources.”
- “If you are unsure, say ‘I don’t know’.”
- “Do not make up information.”

**Few‑shot examples**
- Provide examples of correct, well‑sourced answers
- Show model the desired style and level of certainty

**Chain‑of‑thought (CoT)**
- Force model to reason step‑by‑step
- Easier to spot logical errors
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
**Self‑reflection prompts**
- “Check your answer for factual errors.”
- “Is there any part of this that might be incorrect?”

**Hybrid approaches**
- Combine with web search (e.g., Bing Chat, Perplexity)
- Use tools (calculator, code interpreter) for factual tasks

**Temperature and sampling**
- Lower temperature → less creative, more deterministic
- Top‑p/top‑k sampling → reduce randomness
:::
:::
:::

## The role of the user

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Users can [reduce hallucination risk]{.alert} by:
  - Asking for sources
  - Verifying critical information independently
  - Using specialised tools (e.g., Wolfram Alpha for maths)
  - Being aware of model limitations
- **Critical thinking** is still essential
  - Treat LLM outputs as [starting points]{.alert}, not final answers
  - Cross‑check with trusted references
  - Understand the model’s confidence (or lack thereof)
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![User verification loop](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [OpenAI Help](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8313428-does-chatgpt-tell-the-truth)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# The creative side 🌟 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## When hallucinations are beneficial

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Creative writing**: Poetry, fiction, brainstorming
- **Ideation**: Generating novel concepts, product names, marketing slogans
- **Hypothetical scenarios**: “What if…” explorations
- **Art and design**: Unconstrained visual or musical ideas
- **Humour**: Jokes, puns, absurdist content
- **Education**: Simplifying complex topics (with appropriate caveats)
- **Role‑playing**: Game characters, historical simulations
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Creative writing with AI](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [Medium](https://medium.com/@writingcooperative/how-ai-is-changing-creative-writing-7c3d3b3b3b3b)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Encouraging creativity while managing risk

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Context‑aware prompting**: Signal when creativity is desired
  - “Write a fictional story about…”
  - “Brainstorm possible solutions…”
- **Controlled randomness**: Adjust temperature and sampling parameters
- **Hybrid human‑AI workflows**: Human edits and curates AI‑generated content
- **Ethical guidelines**: Disclose AI involvement, avoid deception
- **Domain‑specific tools**: Use creative‑focused models (e.g., DALL·E for images)
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Creativity vs accuracy trade‑off](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [Jiang et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06647)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Future directions 🚀 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Research frontiers

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Better grounding**: Connect LLMs to real‑world sensors, databases, and tools
- **Self‑correction**: Models that detect and fix their own hallucinations
- **Uncertainty quantification**: Output confidence scores for each claim
- **Multimodal verification**: Use images, audio, and video to verify text
- **Adversarial training**: Expose models to tricky questions that induce hallucinations
- **Causal reasoning**: Move beyond correlation to understand cause‑effect
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Future research directions](figures/placeholder.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/placeholder.png"}

Source: [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06647)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Practical advice for developers

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
**When accuracy is critical**
- Use RAG with up‑to‑date knowledge bases
- Implement human‑in‑the‑loop verification
- Provide clear disclaimers about potential errors
- Log and audit model outputs

**When creativity is desired**
- Encourage diversity with higher temperature
- Use prompt templates that invite exploration
- Combine multiple AI‑generated ideas
- Curate and refine outputs
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
**General best practices**
- Know your model’s strengths and weaknesses
- Test extensively on edge cases
- Monitor for drift and degradation over time
- Stay updated on latest mitigation techniques
- Educate users about limitations
:::
:::
:::

# Summary 📚 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Main takeaways

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 30px;"}

- `r fa('exclamation-triangle')` [Hallucinations]{.alert} are plausible but incorrect outputs, a major challenge for LLMs

- `r fa('balance-scale')` The [creativity–hallucination spectrum]{.alert}: the same mechanism can be a bug or a feature

- `r fa('search')` [Types]{.alert}: factual, logical, coherence, intentional vs. unintentional

- `r fa('ruler')` [Measuring]{.alert} hallucinations is hard—human evaluation, automatic metrics, benchmarks

- `r fa('shield-alt')` [Mitigation]{.alert}: RAG, fine‑tuning, prompt engineering, and user vigilance

- `r fa('lightbulb')` [Creativity]{.alert} can be harnessed while managing risks with context‑aware prompting

- `r fa('road')` [Future work]{.alert}: better grounding, self‑correction, uncertainty quantification
:::
